title: India's Government Health Spending Triples to Rs 4.14 Lakh Crore, Household Share Falls to 42.7%
excerpt: National Health Accounts 2023-24 show government expenditure up threefold since 2013-14 and out-of-pocket spending down 21.5 percentage points as a share of the total — though per-person household payments still rose.
body:
• Government health expenditure in India rose from Rs 1,29,778 crore in 2013-14 to Rs 4,14,196 crore in 2023-24, a threefold increase, according to the National Health Accounts Estimates for India 2023-24 released by the Union Health Ministry on November 15.
  • Out-of-pocket expenditure — what households pay directly — fell from 64.2% of total health expenditure in 2013-14 to 42.7% in 2023-24, a drop of 21.5 percentage points.
  • Per capita government health spending rose from Rs 1,042 to Rs 2,959 over the decade, about 2.8 times higher.
  • The falling share does not mean household bills fell: estimated out-of-pocket spending per person rose from Rs 2,767 in 2022-23 to Rs 2,901 in 2023-24, because total health spending grew faster.

India's government health expenditure has more than tripled in a decade, while the share of health spending that households pay directly out of pocket has fallen sharply, according to the National Health Accounts Estimates for India 2023-24, released by the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on November 15 and reported by ANI.

Government health expenditure increased from Rs 1,29,778 crore in 2013-14 to Rs 4,14,196 crore in 2023-24. Over the same decade, out-of-pocket expenditure as a share of total health expenditure declined from 64.2% to 42.7%, a reduction of 21.5 percentage points, including a fall from 43.4% in 2022-23 to 42.7% in 2023-24.

How the financing mix shifted

The government's share of total health expenditure rose by 14.9 percentage points over the decade. The report estimates India's total health expenditure at Rs 9.52 lakh crore in 2023-24, equivalent to 3.29% of GDP, or Rs 6,801 per person, with government health expenditure amounting to 1.43% of GDP. Government spending on primary healthcare reached approximately Rs 1.53 lakh crore in 2023-24.

Social security expenditure on health — which includes government-financed insurance schemes such as Ayushman Bharat-Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, state health insurance schemes, social health insurance and medical reimbursement for government employees — rose from 6% of total health expenditure in 2013-14 to 11% in 2023-24. Private health insurance expenditure also increased, from 3.4% to 10.2% of total health expenditure over the same period.

The ministry's release linked the shift to initiatives including the expansion of Ayushman Arogya Mandirs for primary care, the Free Drugs and Diagnostics Initiatives, the Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme, the Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana and AMRIT pharmacies, alongside pharmaceutical price regulation by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority.

A smaller share is not the same as a smaller bill

The headline percentage needs one caution, set out in an analysis of the same accounts by MakhanaMornings: a financing share can fall while the amount paid rises, if the overall spending total grows faster. The accounts estimate households' direct health payments at Rs 4,06,197 crore in 2023-24, and out-of-pocket spending per person rose from Rs 2,767 in 2022-23 to Rs 2,901 in 2023-24 at current prices. That per-person figure is a national average across the population, not a typical bill for a patient or a hospital visit.

The same analysis notes that the government figure is not the Union government's spending alone: the report assigns approximately 32% of government health expenditure to the Union and 68% to the states. The estimates are also a picture of 2023-24, prepared from administrative records and surveys — not a reading of what households are paying in November 2026.

What the accounts are

The National Health Accounts Estimates for India 2023-24 are the eleventh round of estimates prepared by the National Health Accounts Technical Secretariat at the National Health Systems Resource Centre, under the Health Ministry. They are prepared using the internationally recognised System of Health Accounts 2011 framework, which tracks how money flows through the health system.

For families in India — and for diaspora readers who help pay for parents' care back home — the direction in the data is a structural one: a larger share of healthcare is now financed through government resources and insurance arrangements, and a smaller share directly by households than a decade ago, even though the average amount households pay has not fallen. Whether that protection reaches the families facing the largest bills relative to their income is a question the aggregate accounts cannot answer on their own.
nri_angle: Diaspora readers who fund parents' medical care in India are directly affected by how much of India's health spending households still pay out of pocket.
